newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean gold firm, underpinned by won rally.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean gold firm, underpinned by won rally.

text.p: Domestic South Korean gold prices remain firm this week on good demand supported by the won's rally against the dollar and on tight supply, dealers in Seoul said on Tuesday.
The domestic currency's rise against the U.S. unit, sparked by continued dollar selling intervention by the central Bank of Korea boosted local gold prices, dealers said.

Gold producer LG Metals' daily selling price for the precious metal, which is regarded as a benchmark for the local bullion wholesale market, rose on Tuesday to 10,200 won per gram from 10,100 a week ago.
But the company's silver price has fallen by three won a gram to 160 won in the past week.

Supplies of largely smuggled gold are tight due to increased security sparked by hightened tensions between North and South Korea, which flared up after the defection of a top official from the North in Beijing and the shooting of a prominent North Korean defector near Seoul.

South Korea has placed its police force on full alert and tighened customs checks after Li Il-nam, who defected to Seoul in 1982, was shot and seriously wounded by suspected North Korean agents near Seoul.
"We believe the tension has curbed gold imports from North Korea. Sharper security also makes it harder to smuggle gold into the country," a dealer said.
The dealer said most South Korean companies prefered to import North Korean gold because products from North Korea are exempt from a three percent import tax.
South Korea's gold imports from North Korea were estimated at between five to six tonnes a year, dealers said.
The won's rise is expected to boost gold demand ahead of the upcoming wedding season, which traditionally starts in March, analysts said.

Gold demand had been weak because of the won's plunge to 84-month lows against the dollar over the past several months. The won had struggled against the dollar's strength on the world market and South Korea's widening current acount deficit.
South Korea posted a record current account deficit of $23.72 billion in 1996, compared to a shortfall of $8.95 billion in 1995, central bank figures showed.
The telegraphic transfer selling rate for customers, posted by the Korea Exchange Bank, fell sharply to 867.80 won against the dollar from 882.30 a week ago.
The rate is regarded as a benchmark for local foreign exchange rates for companies.
